cards.title: In C, what is a memory **address**?
cards.body:
The number that names one byte of memory: byte 0, byte 1, byte 2, and so on.

Think of memory as one very long row of numbered boxes, each holding one byte. The number on a box is its address. A variable that needs several bytes, such as a 4-byte `int`, occupies several boxes in a row, and its address is the address of the first one.

Why it matters: Every variable and every function you write lives at some address. Pointers are how C lets you work with those numbers directly.

Tip: Addresses are normally written in hexadecimal, for example `0x20000400`, because that is easier to read than a long decimal number.

cards.title: In C, what is a **pointer**?
cards.body:
A variable whose value is a memory address.

An `int` variable holds a number. A pointer variable holds the address of some other variable, so it "points to" that variable. Through the pointer you can read or change what lives at that address.

Example: If `x` is stored at address `0x2000`, then a pointer `p` that points to `x` holds the value `0x2000`. The pointer is itself a variable with its own address.

Key idea: A pointer stores where something is, not what it is.
cards.searchQuery: C pointer definition variable holds address

cards.title: Why does every C pointer have a **pointer type** such as `int *` or `char *`, when it only holds an address?
cards.body:
The type tells the compiler how many bytes to access and how to interpret them when you dereference the pointer.

An address alone says where something starts, not how big it is. An `int *` says "an `int` lives here", so `*p` reads 4 bytes (with a 32-bit `int`) as a signed integer. A `char *` says "a `char` lives here", so `*p` reads 1 byte.

Why: The same address can be read in different ways. The pointer type is what picks the way.

Watch out: A plain address carries no size. Mixing up pointer types is how you read the wrong number of bytes.

Why: `p` and `x` are two ways to reach the same bytes. Changing one is visible through the other.

Watch out: The `*` in the declaration `int *p` is part of the type. The `*` in `*p = 9` is the dereference operator. Same symbol, different jobs.

cards.title: In C, what does **pointer arithmetic** mean when you add an integer $n$ to a pointer `p`?
cards.body:
`p + n` points $n$ elements past `p`, which is $n \times$ `sizeof(*p)` bytes further on.

C scales the step by the size of the thing the pointer points to. If `p` is an `int *` and `int` is 4 bytes, then `p + 1` is 4 bytes after `p`, and `p + 3` is 12 bytes after.

Why: You almost always want "the next element", not "the next byte". Scaling by the element size means the same expression works for any element type.

Watch out: Arithmetic is only meaningful inside one array (or one past its end). Stepping elsewhere is undefined behavior.

cards.title: What is **array decay** in C?
cards.body:
In most expressions, including a function call, an array's name turns into a pointer to its first element.

Given `int a[4];`, the expression `a` usually means `&a[0]`, of type `int *`. That is why passing an array to a function really passes only a pointer: the function receives no copy and no length.

Example: The calls `f(a)` and `f(&a[0])` pass exactly the same thing.

Watch out: Two places where the array does not decay are `sizeof a` and `&a`. They still see the whole array.

cards.title: How does C compute the **element address** of `a[i]`, given the array's base address?
cards.body:
Base address $+\ i \times$ `sizeof(a[0])`; in pointer form that is `a + i`, so `a[i]` means `*(a + i)`.

The compiler multiplies the index by the element size and adds that to the base. Because `a + i` is itself pointer arithmetic, indexing is just a dereference of a computed pointer.

Example: With `int32_t a[]` starting at `0x1000`, element 3 lives at $0x1000 + 3 \times 4 =$ `0x100C`.

Why it matters: This is why array indices start at 0. Element 0 sits at offset $0 \times$ `sizeof` from the base.

cards.title: Why is it false that `sizeof(arr)` inside `void f(int arr[])` gives the size of the caller's array?
cards.body:
Because the parameter `int arr[]` is really `int *arr`, so `sizeof(arr)` is the size of a pointer.

The array decayed to a pointer at the call. Inside `f` the length is gone. On a 32-bit Cortex-M, an `int a[4]` in the caller has `sizeof(a)` of 16, but `sizeof(arr)` inside `f` is 4.

Why: C passes only the address of the first element, so the function cannot tell how many elements follow.

Tip: Pass the length as a second parameter, as in `void f(int *arr, size_t n)`. In the caller, `sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0])` still gives the element count.

Why: Indexing works on any pointer, not just on array names.

cards.title: On a 32-bit Cortex-M, `int32_t arr[6];` with `int32_t *p = &arr[1];` and `int32_t *q = &arr[5];`. What is `q - p`, and how many bytes apart are the two addresses?
cards.body:
`q - p` is 4 elements, and the addresses are 16 bytes apart.

Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them: $5 - 1 = 4$. Each `int32_t` is 4 bytes, so the byte distance is $4 \times 4 = 16$.

Why: Pointer subtraction is the reverse of pointer addition: `p + (q - p)` equals `q`. The result is a signed integer type (`ptrdiff_t`).

Watch out: To get the byte distance you must convert the pointers first, for example by casting both to `char *` before subtracting.

cards.title: When do you use `.` and when `->` for **member access** in C?
cards.body:
Use `.` on a struct object and `->` on a pointer to a struct: `p->x` means `(*p).x`.

The arrow first follows the pointer and then picks the member, so it saves you the parentheses. They are needed in `(*p).x` because `.` binds tighter than `*`, so `*p.x` would be read as `*(p.x)`.

Example: With `struct Point pt;` and `struct Point *p = &pt;`, the expressions `pt.x`, `p->x` and `(*p).x` all name the same member.

Watch out: Using `.` on a pointer, or `->` on a struct object, is a compile error. That error is the sign you mixed them up.

cards.title: What are **alignment** and **padding** in a C struct?
cards.body:
Alignment is the rule that an object sits at an address that is a multiple of its alignment requirement (for a basic type, usually its size); padding is the unused bytes the compiler adds to obey it.

A `uint32_t` has to start at a multiple of 4, a `uint16_t` at a multiple of 2, a `uint8_t` anywhere. The compiler inserts padding bytes between members so each member is aligned, and at the end so the struct's size is a multiple of its strictest member's alignment.

Why: Some CPUs fault on a misaligned access (for example a Cortex-M0 on a 32-bit load), and others are slower. Alignment keeps each access to one clean transfer.

Watch out: Padding is invisible in the source but counts in `sizeof`, in memory use and in anything that copies the struct byte by byte.

cards.title: In C, what is a **union**, and how big is it?
cards.body:
A union is a type whose members all share the same memory, so it is as big as its largest member (plus any padding).

Writing one member overwrites the bytes the others use. A union is for "one of these alternatives at a time", or for looking at the same bytes in two ways.

Example: In `union U { uint32_t w; uint8_t b[4]; };` the 4-byte `w` and the 4-element `b` occupy the same 4 bytes, so `sizeof(union U)` is 4.

Tip: Embedded code often wraps a union and a tag field in a struct, so the tag records which alternative is currently valid.

cards.title: You are writing a driver for a hardware control register whose fields sit at fixed bit positions. Do you describe it with C **bit-fields** in a struct, or with shifts and masks on a `uint32_t`?
cards.body:
Shifts and masks win for registers, because the layout of a C bit-field is up to the compiler.

A **bit-field** is a struct member declared with a width in bits, such as `unsigned mode : 3;`. The standard leaves much about them to the compiler to choose and document: whether the first field sits at the low or the high end of the word, how fields are packed into the storage unit, and whether a plain `int` field is signed. A compiler may also access the register with a different width than the hardware expects.

Bit-fields do read nicely, and a driver tied to one known compiler can use them. Some vendor headers do.

Why it matters: A masked version, such as `(reg >> 4) & 0x7`, behaves the same on every compiler.

Tip: Reserve bit-fields for data private to your program, where you do not care about the bit layout.

cards.title: What are the five regions of a C program's **memory layout**, in the usual order from low to high addresses?
cards.body:
Text (the code), data, bss, the heap, then the stack at the top.

The **text segment** holds the machine code. The **data segment** holds globals and statics that start with a non-zero value. The **bss** holds the ones that start at zero. The **heap** grows upward as you ask for memory, and the **stack** grows downward from the top of the address space.

Example: On a microcontroller, the text and the initial values for the data live in flash. At startup, code copies those values into RAM and zeroes the bss. The heap and stack share the rest of the RAM.

Why it matters: Heap and stack grow toward each other. If either runs too far, it corrupts the other.

cards.title: What is the **bss**, and which variables end up there?
cards.body:
The bss is the region for global and static variables that start at zero (or have no initializer); it takes no space in the program file.

Because every byte starts at zero, the file only needs to record how big the region is. The startup code zeroes that much RAM before `main` runs.

Example: `int total;` and `static int count = 0;` go to the bss, while `int limit = 5;` goes to the data segment, because its starting value must be stored in the file.

Why it matters: On a microcontroller this means large zero-initialized arrays cost RAM but no flash.

cards.title: What is a **stack frame**?
cards.body:
The block of stack memory that one function call uses for its local variables, saved registers and return address.

A frame is created when a function is called and thrown away when it returns. Each new call puts its frame on top of the caller's frame, so the stack is a last-in, first-out pile.

Why: This is why each call to a recursive function gets its own copy of the local variables, and why locals vanish when the function returns.

Key idea: The cost of a call is a frame, and frames add up as calls nest.

cards.title: What is the **heap**, and who decides how long its memory lives?
cards.body:
The heap is the region from which a program requests blocks at run time; the program itself decides when each block is released.

A call such as `malloc(n)` reserves `n` bytes of heap and hands back a pointer to them. That block stays valid until the program gives it back, no matter which function made the request. This is unlike a local variable, which dies when its function returns.

Tip: Both lifetime and size are chosen at run time. That freedom is the reason for the heap, and the reason it needs care.

cards.body:
Three frames exist (`main`, `f`, `g`), and `g`'s frame is removed first.

`main` calls `f`, which puts its frame on top of `main`'s. `f` calls `g`, whose frame goes on top again. When `g` returns, its frame is popped; then `f`'s; then `main`'s. The most recent call finishes first.

Why it matters: The deepest chain of calls sets the most stack the program ever needs. Estimating that depth is how you size a stack on a microcontroller.

Watch out: A recursive function adds one frame per level, so a deep recursion can use much more stack than its source suggests.

cards.title: Why is it false that an ordinary local `int count = 0;` followed by `count++;` remembers its value from one call to the next?
cards.body:
Because an ordinary local has automatic storage: it is created fresh on each call and destroyed on return.

Every call re-runs `int count = 0;` on a new copy, so the old value is gone. To keep a value between calls, declare the variable `static`. A **static** local has **static storage**: one copy for the whole run of the program, set up before `main` starts.

Example: A function with `static int n = 0; n++; return n;` returns 1, 2, 3 on three calls. With a plain `int n` it returns 1 every time.

Watch out: A static local lives in the data or bss region, not on the stack, and all callers share it.

- Make `x` `static`, so it survives the return.

cards.title: A function on a 4 KiB-stack microcontroller needs a 2 KiB scratch buffer while it runs. Should the buffer be a local array, a `static` array or heap memory?
cards.body:
A `static` array: it adds no stack pressure and its size is fixed at build time.

A 2 KiB local would use half the stack, and one deeper call chain overflows it. A heap block can fail at run time, and how long it takes to get is hard to predict. A static array's size shows up in the build's memory report, so you know before the device ships whether it fits.

The other side: A static buffer occupies RAM all the time, even when the function is idle, and the function is no longer safe to call from two tasks or an interrupt at once. A local array is released automatically on return and is safe when several tasks call the function at once.

Tip: Prefer static or global buffers for large, fixed-size work areas on small targets.

cards.title: What does `malloc` do, what does it return, and what are the contents of what it returns?
cards.body:
`void *malloc(size_t size)` reserves `size` bytes on the heap and returns a pointer to them, or `NULL` if it cannot; the bytes are uninitialised.

Declared in `<stdlib.h>`. Because it returns `void *`, you can assign the result to any pointer type in C without a cast. The block holds whatever bytes were there before, so you must write to it before you read it.

Example: `int *a = malloc(10 * sizeof *a);` asks for room for 10 ints. Writing `sizeof *a` keeps the size right even if you later change the type of `a`.

Watch out: Always test the result against `NULL` before using it. On a small device, running out is a real possibility.

cards.title: What must be true of a pointer you pass to `free`, and how many times may you do it?
cards.body:
It must be exactly the pointer that `malloc`, `calloc` or `realloc` returned (or `NULL`), and it may be freed only once.

`free(p)` returns the block to the allocator so it can be handed out again. Passing `NULL` is allowed and does nothing. Passing a pointer into the middle of a block, a pointer to a local variable, or the same pointer a second time is undefined behavior.

Key idea: Every successful allocation needs exactly one matching `free`. Fewer leaks memory, more corrupts it.

Tip: Decide for each block which part of the program owns it. The owner is the one that frees it.

cards.title: What is a **memory leak**?
cards.body:
A heap block that was allocated and never freed, so that the program can no longer reach it or reuse it.

The block stays reserved until the program ends, and once the last pointer to it is lost nothing can ever free it. One small leak is harmless. A leak on every pass of a loop or every message received slowly uses up the heap.

Example: A device leaks 32 bytes per message and receives 10 messages a second. A 64 KiB heap holds 65,536 bytes, and the leak uses 320 bytes a second, so the heap is gone in about 205 s, a little over 3 minutes.

Why it matters: Leaks matter most on devices that run for months without a restart.

cards.title: Why is it false that after `free(p)` the pointer `p` is `NULL` or otherwise safe to use?
cards.body:
Because `free` releases the block but leaves `p` unchanged, so `p` becomes a dangling pointer.

A **dangling pointer** holds the address of memory that is no longer yours. Reading or writing through it is a **use-after-free**, which is undefined behavior. It may seem to work for a while, because the old bytes are often still there, and then fail later when the allocator reuses the block.

Fix: Set the pointer to `NULL` right after freeing it.

```c
free(p);
p = NULL;
```

Watch out: Any other copy of the pointer is still dangling. Setting `p = NULL` also turns an accidental second `free(p)` into a harmless no-op.

cards.title: For firmware that must run for months, do you allocate buffers with `malloc` while running, or allocate everything at start-up (or statically)?
cards.body:
Allocate at start-up or statically: it removes run-time allocation failures and a timing cost you cannot predict.

A running device cannot recover well from `malloc` returning `NULL` at a bad moment. The time a `malloc` takes can vary with the heap's state, which is a problem when a deadline must be met. Long uptimes also invite fragmentation. Coding standards such as MISRA C:2012 (rule 21.3) forbid `malloc` and `free` for these reasons.

The other side: Static sizing has to reserve for the worst case, which wastes RAM when the average is far lower. Dynamic allocation is flexible when sizes are truly unknown.

Tip: A common compromise is to allocate during start-up and never `free` afterwards.

cards.title: A device creates and destroys thousands of identical 64-byte message objects over weeks. Do you use general `malloc` and `free`, or a **fixed-size block pool**?
cards.body:
A fixed-size block pool: every block is interchangeable, so **fragmentation** cannot stop an allocation.

Fragmentation means that enough memory is free in total but split into holes too small for the request. Example: two free holes of 50 bytes cannot serve a 64-byte request, although 100 bytes are free. In a pool every free block fits every request, and allocating and freeing take a short, fixed time.

The other side: A pool serves one block size, so objects of other sizes need their own pool, and a pool's reserved memory is not available to anything else. General `malloc` suits objects with widely varying sizes and short runs.

Key idea: Make all blocks the same size and holes stop mattering.

cards.title: What is a **bit mask**?
cards.body:
A value whose 1 bits mark which bits of another value an operation should affect.

You combine the mask with the data using `&`, `|` or `^`. A 1 in the mask means "this bit is in play"; a 0 means "leave it alone".

Example: To keep only the low nibble of a byte, AND with the mask `0x0F`. The byte `0xB5` becomes `0x05`, because the upper four bits are masked off.

Why it matters: Hardware registers pack many separate settings into one word. Masks are how code reads or changes one setting without disturbing the others.

cards.title: How do you **set**, **clear**, **toggle** and test bit `n` of an unsigned integer `x` in C?
cards.body:
Set: `x |= (1u << n);` Clear: `x &= ~(1u << n);` Toggle: `x ^= (1u << n);` Test: `(x >> n) & 1u`.

The expression `1u << n` builds a mask with only bit `n` on. OR with that mask forces the bit to 1. AND with its complement `~` forces it to 0 and leaves every other bit as it was. XOR flips the bit. To test, shift the bit down to position 0 and mask off the rest.

Mnemonic: OR sets, AND-NOT clears, XOR flips.

Watch out: Clearing needs the inverted mask. `x &= (1u << n)` would instead wipe every other bit.

Because `1` is a signed `int`, and shifting a 1 into its sign bit overflows; the result is not representable, so it is undefined behavior. Write `1u << 31`.

Bit operations are only safely defined on unsigned types. The value $2^{31}$ does not fit in a 32-bit signed `int`. With `1u` the shift happens in `unsigned int`, where the result $2^{31}$ is `0x80000000` and is well defined.

Why it matters: A mask for the top bit is common in flag words and registers. The bug often hides until a compiler or option changes how the expression is folded.

Tip: Make `u` a habit: `1u << n`, and use `UINT32_C(1)` or `1ul` when you need a wider constant.

cards.title: What is a **read-modify-write** update of a register or word?
cards.body:
Read the whole word, change only the bits you mean to change, and write the whole word back.

You cannot normally write a single bit to a 32-bit register. The write replaces all 32 bits, so you first read the current value, apply a mask to change just your field, and store the result.

Example: `reg |= (1u << 3);` is a read-modify-write: it reads `reg`, ORs in bit 3 and writes the result back.

Watch out: The three steps are not one uninterruptible step. If an interrupt changes the same register between the read and the write, its change can be overwritten.

- `enable = (r >> 7) & 1u;`

cards.title: What does the `volatile` qualifier tell the C compiler?
cards.body:
That the object can change, or be observed, outside the program's own flow, so every access written in the source must really happen, in order.

For a `volatile` object the compiler may not keep its value in a CPU register between uses, merge two reads into one, drop a write whose value is never read back, or reorder it against other `volatile` accesses.

Why it matters: A hardware register changes by itself, and writing to it can start an action. Treating it as ordinary memory breaks both.

Example: `volatile uint32_t *p;` declares a pointer to a `uint32_t` that must be accessed exactly as the code says.

cards.title: What is a **memory-mapped register** in a microcontroller?
cards.body:
A control or status register of a peripheral that appears at a fixed address in the ordinary address space, so ordinary loads and stores reach it.

Reading it may return the state of the hardware, such as "transfer finished", and writing it sets the hardware's behavior or starts an action. The address, called the **register address**, is given in the chip's reference manual, and it never changes at run time.

Example: To switch on an LED, firmware stores a 1 to the bit of an output register at one agreed address.

Key idea: To the program a register looks like a variable, but to the hardware it is a lever or a gauge.

Because the compiler assumes memory changes only when the program itself changes it, so it reads `STATUS` once and reuses that value.

Nothing inside the **polling loop** writes to `STATUS`, so the compiler concludes that the value cannot change between passes. It loads the register once, and then either skips the loop or spins on the old value forever.

Why: The optimizer knows nothing about the hardware. `volatile` is how you tell it that the memory has an outside life.

Example: At `-O2` the compiler emits a single load and then a branch to itself. At `-O0` the same code often works, which is why this bug shows up only in release builds.

Because `volatile` affects only what the compiler may do; it does not make the operation atomic or order it against another core.

**Atomicity** means an operation happens as one indivisible step. `counter++` on a `volatile int` is still three steps: read, add 1, write. An interrupt (or another core) that changes `counter` between the read and the write has its update lost.

Likewise `volatile` does not tell the processor or its caches to keep accesses in order between cores.

Example: A timer driver might have `timer_start(period, on_tick, &state)`. When the period ends, it calls `on_tick(&state)`.

cards.title: What is **undefined behavior** (UB) in C?
cards.body:
Code for which the C standard places no requirements at all, so the program may do anything.

The program might crash, give a wrong answer, appear to work, or behave differently after you change the optimization level or the compiler. The standard puts no limit on what the program as a whole may do.

Example: Reading past the end of an array, dereferencing `NULL`, dividing by zero and overflowing a signed integer are all undefined.

Why it matters: UB is a bug even when the program "works on my machine". The compiler is allowed to break it at any time.

Key idea: UB is not an error message. The compiler does not have to tell you.

cards.title: How do **implementation-defined**, **unspecified** and undefined behavior differ, with an example of each?
cards.body:
Implementation-defined: the compiler picks and must document it. Unspecified: one of several valid outcomes, with no documentation required. Undefined: no requirements at all.

- Implementation-defined: the size of `int`, or whether plain `char` is signed (on a typical 64-bit desktop it is; in GCC for Arm Cortex-M it is not).
- Unspecified: the order in which the arguments of `f(g(), h())` are evaluated. Either order is valid, but you cannot rely on one.
- Undefined: signed integer overflow, or `*p` with `p == NULL`.

Why it matters: The first two are portability traps, since the program stays valid but means different things on different targets. The third makes the whole program invalid.

cards.title: What does the **strict aliasing** rule say?
cards.body:
An object may be accessed only through an lvalue of its own type (or a compatible one), or through a character type; accessing it as an unrelated type is undefined behavior.

Because of this rule the compiler assumes that a pointer to `float` and a pointer to `int` never refer to the same memory. It may therefore keep values in registers and reorder loads and stores accordingly.

Example: Writing through an `int *` and then reading the same bytes through a `float *` can give a stale result at `-O2`.

Watch out: Casting a pointer to another type and dereferencing it is the usual way to break the rule. Copying with `memcpy` or reading through `unsigned char *` is allowed.

cards.title: Why is it false that undefined behavior only makes the one faulty operation give an unpredictable result?
cards.body:
Because the compiler is allowed to assume UB never happens, so it can change or delete code anywhere that relies on that assumption.

A faulty operation can therefore make a check vanish, make a loop run wrongly or make other code behave oddly. The damage need not stay near the line where the bug is.

Example: If the code uses a pointer and later tests it against `NULL`, the compiler may reason "it was already dereferenced, so it cannot be `NULL`" and delete the test.

Key idea: With UB you cannot reason about what the machine would do. You must remove the UB.

cards.body:
It may compile to `return 0;`; the correct check is `x == INT_MAX` (from `<limits.h>`).

**Signed integer overflow** is undefined, so the compiler may assume `x + 1` never overflows. Under that assumption `x + 1 < x` is always false, and the whole function folds to a constant 0. At `-O2` Clang does exactly this.

The same check on an `unsigned` value is fine: unsigned arithmetic wraps by definition.

Why it matters: The two's-complement wrap-around you know from the hardware does not carry over to signed `int` in C.

Tip: Test before the operation, not after it: `if (a > 0 && x > INT_MAX - a)` checks that `x + a` would overflow.

cards.body:
An **uninitialised variable** is read when `argc <= 5`, which is undefined; `-Wall -Wextra` can warn.

An automatic variable has no starting value. If the `if` is false, `x` still holds whatever was left in that stack slot (or register), so the program prints garbage that can change from run to run. Clang names it `-Wsometimes-uninitialized`; GCC reports `-Wmaybe-uninitialized` when optimizing.

Watch out: UBSan does not catch this. To find uninitialised reads at run time, use Valgrind or, with Clang on supported platforms, MemorySanitizer.

Tip: Initialize at the declaration: `int x = 0;`. The warning then disappears for the right reason.

cards.body:
It breaks the strict aliasing rule (a `float` is read as a `uint32_t`); copy the bytes instead: `memcpy(&u, &f, sizeof u);`.

The cast pointer `uint32_t *` is dereferenced to access an object of type `float`, which is undefined. It often works at low optimization and then breaks when the compiler decides that a store to `f` cannot affect a read through a `uint32_t *`.

The `memcpy` version is defined, and compilers turn it into a single register move. For `1.0f` it gives `0x3f800000`.

Tip: A union can also read the bits, as in the earlier type-punning card. `memcpy` is the most portable of these.

cards.body:
A message like `runtime error: index 4 out of bounds for type 'int[4]'`, with the file and line.

UBSan, the Undefined Behavior Sanitizer, adds checks to the compiled program for many kinds of undefined behavior, such as array bounds, signed overflow, bad shifts and misaligned pointers. When one fires, it prints where. Without it, this program would most likely print 0 and look fine.

Why it matters: Silent UB is the dangerous kind. Run your tests with `-fsanitize=undefined` (often combined with `-fsanitize=address`) and with `-Wall -Wextra` on a normal build.

Tip: Compile with `-g` for useful line numbers.

cards.title: Your firmware is stable in testing. Do you ship the production build with `-fsanitize=undefined` still enabled, or run the sanitizer only in test builds?
cards.body:
Run UBSan in host and test builds (and CI), and ship without it, unless the device has code space, RAM and time to spare.

The checks add code, slow execution and normally need a run-time support library and a way to print messages, none of which suits a small flash and a hard deadline. Test builds see most of the same bugs at no cost to the product.

The other side: Production keeps the safety net. Trap-on-error modes exist in both Clang and GCC and are smaller, so they are sometimes used on safety-relevant code, at a still real cost in size.

Tip: Keep `-Wall -Wextra` on in every build. Warnings cost nothing at run time.
